title: the sound the universe hums
hook: a boy waits three days at Death's door and is given one word: om
tomorrow: the prayer you know by heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha, the one who goes first. Today, the sound that opens almost every Hindu prayer.

Om. A yoga class ends with it, and Hindu prayers begin with it. To see why, start with a boy who walked to Death's door. His father, in a temper, shouted at him: I give you to Death. So Nachiketa went. Death wasn't home. The boy waited at the door for three days without food, and when Death came back, ashamed to have kept a guest hungry, he offered him three wishes.
screen: `OM.` → `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `THREE DAYS. THREE WISHES.`

segments.voice: For the third wish, Nachiketa asked the biggest question there is: what happens to us after we die? Death tried to talk him out of it. Take gold, he said. Horses, kingdoms, a long life. The boy said no: all of that ends. So Death taught him, and at the heart of the teaching was one word. The word every sacred text points to, Death said, is om. This syllable is Brahman: the one reality underneath everything. That's the big idea inside the sound. For Hindus, om isn't a hum. It's the name of the whole. Another short, old text says om is all of this, past, present and future, and hears four parts in it. A: waking, the world you can touch. U: dreaming. M: deep, dreamless sleep. And the fourth has no sound. It's the silence after the m runs out, and the text calls it the self, at peace. That's why prayers, mantras and readings of scripture begin with om. Before you ask for anything small, you name the whole. So the next time a room goes quiet before om, you'll know what's happening: everything is being named before anything is asked.
screen: `THE BIGGEST QUESTION.` · `OM IS BRAHMAN: THE WHOLE.` · `A, U, M — AND THE SILENCE.` · `NAME THE WHOLE FIRST.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. Let it out as the sound, aloud or under your breath: a, u, m. Let the m run out on its own, then stay a second in the quiet after it. That quiet is the fourth part.
Om. A, u and m for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after it for the fourth. Second word on your strand.
screen: `OM — your 2nd word` → clicks onto the strand beside namaste.

segments.voice: Your line: one sound, before words. Not a task. Something to notice the next time a room goes quiet before it begins. Day two, done.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PRAYER YOU KNOW BY HEART.`

howItsDone: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

what a scholar hears: Mandukya Upanishad: a for waking, u for dream, m for deep sleep, and the soundless fourth, called simply the fourth (chaturtha; later teachers call it turiya).

story.title: the boy who waited for Death
story.text: A boy named Nachiketa is sent to Death by his angry father, and he actually goes. Death isn't home, so the boy waits three days at the door without food. To make up for it, Death offers him three wishes. For the third, Nachiketa asks what happens after we die. Death offers him gold, long life, whole kingdoms, anything else instead. The boy says no. So Death teaches him, and at the center of the teaching is a single word: om.

wrong.myth: om is a hum to end a yoga class.
wrong.truth: one of the oldest Hindu texts treats it as a map: a, u and m for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after it as the fourth.

notes: Mandukya verse 1 (om is all this: past, present, future, and beyond the three times) and verses 8–12 (a, u, m as waking, dream, deep sleep; the soundless fourth, peaceful, the self) are paraphrased. Confirm verse numbers and that 'the self, peaceful, where the noise of the world falls away' fairly renders verse 12 (prapanchopashama, shiva, advaita).
Gita 17.24 says that for those who follow Vedic teaching, acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity begin with om; paraphrased as 'offering, giving and discipline'. Confirm.
Cut from manuscript day 2 under the claims rule: 'every yoga class on earth', 'the most-analyzed syllable in human history', the Mandukya being 'about eight hundred words' and 'one of the shortest'.
Title keeps the index ('the sound the universe hums'); the script doesn't claim the universe literally hums. Keeper may want a line on how tradition speaks of om as the primal sound.

Editor pass: hook no longer tells the listener they felt self-conscious ('some people feel'); 'in about ten seconds' cut to 'in a single breath' under the claims rule; Mandukya ref widened to 1, 3–5, 7–12, since the states (waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth) are described in 3–5 and 7 and mapped to a, u, m and the soundless fourth in 8–12.

Editor review 2: trapdoor said the Mandukya calls the fourth 'turiya'; the Mandukya's own word is chaturtha (verses 7, 12), and turiya is the later term (Gaudapada and others), so the floor now says both. Spoken lines read and left as they were.
